Its sound comes from the player's lips vibrating in the mouthpiece, which sets the column of air in the tube in a standing wave; by adjusting lip tension and the amount of breath the player changes pitch, volume and timbre. Its tone is mainly bright: the C trumpet, with its shorter body, sounds more brilliant, the soprano trumpet is one of the highest instruments in the brass family, and the bass trumpet lies an octave below the standard B-flat instrument. Compared with the cornet, the trumpet's body is mostly cylindrical while the cornet's is conical; the shape and depth of the mouthpiece cup also affect the timbre, and the wider and deeper the cup, the darker the sound.

Progress in metalworking in the late Middle Ages and the Renaissance let the valveless natural trumpet play the overtone series and develop the clarino high register, and players such as Cesare Bendinelli brought on the golden age of the Baroque. In the Classical and Romantic periods its standing fell because of the natural trumpet's limits, and Berlioz in 1844 criticised its marginalisation. Once the modern valve appeared the trumpet could play a full chromatic scale, and it became a staple of orchestras, wind bands, jazz and popular music.

The trumpet is a brass aerophone, H-S classification 423.233. It is commonly a B-flat transposing instrument, sounding a whole tone below the written note; the family includes the soprano trumpet and the bass trumpet. A modern trumpet is usually brass tubing bent into a rounded rectangle with three or four valves or rotary valves, pressed to lengthen the body and lower the pitch. The player vibrates the lips in the mouthpiece, setting the air inside the tube in a standing wave. Trumpeters are used in orchestras, wind bands, chamber music, jazz ensembles, popular music and school bands, and the instrument has also served as a war or hunting signal.
